job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Diego Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a graduate scheme at a regional power network firm in Leicester. I studied electrical engineering, and my final project was a fault detector for a street-level transformer. Days are a mix of desk work, modelling load on the grid, and a site visit every week or so with a field engineer called Mo, who treats me like a nephew.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is that the work matters, since people notice when the lights go off. What I don't like is that the loan takes a big bite and that the scheme pays little for the first two years. I have about a week of savings, I share a rented house with two others, and my parents have their own bills, so I'm on my own with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. I use AI now and then to tidy a report or explain a standard, and I'd say it's useful but not magic. I'd tell friends that most of the change is in small boring tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly settled in that world. A power network is slow and regulated, and graduate schemes tend to lead to jobs. What bothers me is money: the scheme pay is low, the loan is high and I can't save much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the scheme, pass my professional review, and try to move into a permanent engineer role. I'd use AI for report drafts and keep an eye on what's allowed under company rules. I'd put 60 a month aside and ask Mo whether there's any overtime on storm duty, which pays extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small worry about money sits in the background, like a light left on in another room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the scheme pay is low. What happens when it ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm kept on, my pay goes up by about a quarter. If I'm not, I'd look at other utilities, but there are few around here, so I might have to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why storm duty overtime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because storms come every winter, and the extra hours add up to a decent top-up. It's also when you learn the most, since everything goes wrong at once.

say: It's **useful but not magic**, and most change is in small boring tasks.
I'd tell friends not to worry.
think: A power network is slow and regulated, so I feel **fairly settled**.
The real worry is low scheme pay against a **high loan**.
do: Finish the scheme and pass my **professional review**.
Use AI for report drafts within company rules.
Save **60 a month** and ask Mo about storm-duty overtime.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with a small money worry like a light left on.

Steady and unhurried; uses AI without fuss.
His mentor Mo anchors his learning.

steps.text: Finish the graduate scheme and sit the professional review
Use AI to draft site reports within company rules
Put 60 a month into savings and take storm-duty overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real shift and that sensible people should adapt. I'd tell friends who do desk jobs to learn the tools now. I'd also say the grid has to stay safe, so there are limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd split my job in two. The modelling and report parts are thinking work that AI takes over, and the site work stays human for longer. So I'd want to do more site work and less spreadsheet work, because that's where the safe future is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move into field operations for a year, and I'd learn how to supervise the automated models, so I can say when they're wrong. I'd take a course on grid control systems. I'd also keep the budget tight, at about 900 a month, and carry on paying down the loan slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert but not afraid. It feels like an exam I know is coming and have time to study for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the grid has to stay safe so there are limits. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a model gets a load forecast wrong, a street goes dark, and that makes the news. So regulators will insist a human checks things, which is a job I could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if work slowed down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, which is only about 40 a month for me. After that, I'd leave my gym and cancel the streaming subscription I share with my housemates.

Take a course on **grid control** systems and learn to check automated models.
Keep monthly spending near **900** and pay the loan slowly.
feel: **Alert but not afraid**, like an exam I have time to study for.

steps.text: Ask for a year in field operations after the scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's crazy fast, and the regulators and the government can't write rules in two years. I'd say we need to slow down and protect people, but I wouldn't expect to be listened to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be worried. Modelling load is thinking work, and a machine would do it overnight. The site work stays for about three years until robots catch up, and after that I'd be a graduate engineer on a short contract with a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd press hard for a place in field operations and take every site shift available. I'd put every spare pound into cash and stop all optional spending. I'd also ask my parents if I could use their spare room for a few months if my housemates and I had to give up the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened and a bit numb. I'd watch the news more than is healthy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take every site shift. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because being the person who's physically there is the one thing I can control. If a transformer is down, a model can't climb the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to Mo about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly. He's been in this for thirty years and he's seen firms cut people in every downturn. He'd tell me where to stand, and I'd listen.

say: It's **crazy fast**, and rules can't be written in two years.
I'd say we should protect people but expect no one to listen.
think: Modelling is **thinking work** a machine does overnight, and site work buys three years.

do: Take every **site shift** and push for field operations.
Move spare money into **cash** and drop optional spending.
Ask my parents about their **spare room**.
feel: **Frightened and numb**, watching the news more than is healthy.
S2.quote: If a transformer is down, a model can't climb the pole.
fieldNote: He expects the desk part to go, but sees a **three-year** window in hands-on work.
Rather than panic, he narrows his focus to what he can control.

steps.text: Take every site shift available and push for field operations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is short but workable. I'd say it's enough time for sensible people to adapt, and I'd tell friends to keep learning, pay down debt and not tie their identity to one skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pressured but not hopeless. I'd have time to finish the scheme, get chartered and move into the part of the job that stays physical. I'd want the loan down by the time 2031 arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go chartered by year three and spend most of those years in field work and protection systems, where people are still needed. I'd pay 150 a month toward the loan. And I'd keep AI tools in my daily work so I stay current with what changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. It's a bit like a long exam period. You can't escape it, but you can prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not move to a different field entirely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my skills fit here, and the grid is a safe place to be if you're physical about it. I'd only move if the firm showed it wanted fewer engineers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the warning sign for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm stopped hiring graduates for the scheme. That's the cheapest way for a company to shrink, and everyone sees it a year before layoffs.

I'd tell friends to keep learning and pay down debt.

feel: **Steady**, like a long exam period you can prepare for.

steps.text: Get chartered by the end of year three
Move into field protection systems work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives plenty of room, and I'd say that out loud. I'd tell friends to not panic, but to use the decade to be good at something solid, and not to waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine. I'd be 32 and I'd have a mid-level job, a house share or maybe my own flat, and a loan almost gone. The risk is if I stand still, and I'd be careful about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the industry, become chartered, and pay off the loan in six or seven years. I'd save for a deposit after that and take one new course every two years. I'd also volunteer for a project on battery storage, because that's where the grid is heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A tiny part of me would still keep a bag packed, if you see what I mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by a bag packed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A back-up plan. I'd keep my CV up to date and my savings fed, so that if things move faster than the card says, I'm not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who's panicking about AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a lot of Mondays. Use them: learn something, save something and stay in touch with people who might hire you.

I'd tell friends to be good at something solid.
think: At 32 I'd be fine, with a **mid-level job** and a nearly cleared loan.

feel: **Calm**, though a small part of me would keep a bag packed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it leaves no time to clear a loan or get chartered. What would help is a government that says clearly what rules it's writing, and firms that keep taking on graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Nothing in particular. Maybe that most people like me aren't doom-minded; we're just trying to make a plan and not be surprised.

headlineQuote: Most people like me aren't doom-minded; we're just trying to make a plan and not be surprised.
